# Validation report

<!-- Generated by smps.report. Do not edit by hand; `make demo` overwrites this file. -->

Every number in this file is produced by `make demo`. The date it was produced
is in the git history, which is a better record than a line in a generated
document that would otherwise change every day for no reason.

## What was validated, and what that word means here

Nothing in this report is a measurement. No board has been fabricated,
assembled, powered or probed. Every figure comes from a model running on a
desktop machine.

What has been checked is the thing the project brief puts first: that the loop
compensation derived by hand produces the crossover and phase margin claimed
for it, when the actual switching converter is simulated cycle by cycle with a
small signal injected into the feedback path and the loop gain extracted the
same way a Bode analyser extracts it.

Two independent routes to the same number:

1. **Hand derived.** Each power stage is written as two linear systems, one per
   switch state, averaged and linearised. For the current mode rails the
   comparator loop is closed with the Ridley sampled data model. The
   compensator is a closed form network response. `docs/compensation/` shows
   the derivation with this board's arithmetic written out.
2. **Simulated.** The same converter run as a switching circuit, with the
   compensator carried as extra states, the switching instant found by root
   finding on the real comparator condition, and the loop gain measured by
   injection.

They share the component values and nothing else. The power stage model in
route 2 does not use route 1's transfer functions.

## Result: the two routes agree

| rail | f_cross_target_hz | f_cross_hand_hz | f_cross_sim_hz | f_cross_error_pct | pm_target_deg | pm_hand_deg | pm_sim_deg | pm_error_deg | gm_hand_db | gm_sim_db | injection_linearity_rel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| +5V | 50000.0 | 49617.8 | 49879.3 | 0.53 | 55.0 | 62.89 | 64.71 | 1.82 | 12.91 | no -180 deg crossing below fsw/2 | 1.12e-04 |
| +3V3 | 100000.0 | 99130.6 | 95509.1 | -3.65 | 55.0 | 65.27 | 69.32 | 4.04 | 16.9 | no -180 deg crossing below fsw/2 | 2.37e-04 |
| +12V | 6000.0 | 5820.2 | 6156.1 | 5.77 | 50.0 | 76.29 | 78.0 | 1.71 | 14.46 | 15.7 | 1.37e-04 |

Worst crossover disagreement 5.8 percent, worst phase margin
disagreement 4.0 degrees. The gate the brief sets, that the
simulation has to match the hand calculation before boards are ordered, is met.

`injection_linearity_rel` is the fractional change in measured loop gain when
the injection amplitude is doubled. Values around 1e-4 mean the measurement is
in the small signal regime, which is the same check a careful bench sweep does.

Where the simulation is expected to differ from the hand model, and does:

* Above roughly a fifth of the switching frequency the averaged model loses
  accuracy because averaging assumes the ripple is small compared with the
  signal being measured. That is visible as the two traces separating at the
  top of each Bode plot.
* The boost disagrees slightly more than the bucks at low frequency. The
  Ridley model drops the input and output voltage feedforward terms in the
  duty cycle modulator, and for a boost those are not quite negligible.
* Neither route models dead time, reverse recovery, gate driver delay or
  layout inductance. All of those cost phase on real hardware, so a bench
  measurement should come in worse than this, not better.

The +5V stage is essentially indifferent to input voltage, which is not an
accident and is worth stating precisely because it looks too good. With peak
current mode and the artificial ramp set to the falling inductor current slope,
the modulator gain goes as 1/Vin while the control to output gain goes as Vin,
and the two cancel exactly in the averaged model. The real converter will not
be perfectly flat, because dead time, gate drive timing and Rds(on) all move
with operating point and none of them are in this model.

Per stage numbers are in `test-results/efficiency/stage_efficiency.csv`. The
+1V8A rail sits near 1.8/3.3 by construction: it is a linear regulator and the
difference is heat, which is the price paid for a quiet analogue supply.

At high line the +5V stage is dominated by switching loss, not conduction loss.
If a bench measurement ever disagrees with this model, that is the term to
suspect first, because the overlap time it depends on is the hardest quantity
to predict from a datasheet.

## Conducted emissions pre-scan

| v_in_v | worst_margin_db | worst_frequency_hz | filter_z_out_peak_ohm | filter_z_out_peak_hz | converter_z_in_ohm | middlebrook_separation_db |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.0 | 4.72 | 500000.0 | 0.5006 | 3147.7 | 2.679 | 14.57 |
| 24.0 | 8.05 | 500000.0 | 0.5006 | 3147.7 | 23.605 | 33.47 |
| 36.0 | 11.2 | 500000.0 | 0.5006 | 3147.7 | 52.298 | 40.38 |

Differential mode only, modelled through a 10 uH input
inductor into a 2.2 uF film capacitor and a 50 ohm / 5 uH LISN.
The worst case is the fundamental at the switching frequency at low line, with
4.7 dB of margin at
Vin 8 V. That is thin for a prediction with this
much uncertainty in it, and it is the first thing a real pre-scan should look
at.

The input filter is also checked against Middlebrook's criterion, because a
converter running closed loop is a constant power load and looks like a
negative resistance below its loop bandwidth. Worst separation between the
filter output impedance and the converter input impedance is
14.6 dB. This is why the bulk
capacitor is an aluminium polymer part with deliberate ESR: swapping it for
more ceramic would improve the ripple and destabilise the input.

## How reproducible is any of this

Every result here is regenerated by `make demo` and compared against what is
committed, by `scripts/check_outputs_current.py`, on every push.

That comparison is numerical rather than byte for byte, and deliberately so.
The switching simulator finds each switching instant by secant iteration on the
real comparator condition, and where that iteration stops depends on the last
bits of a double precision subtraction. The closed loop then integrates the
resulting duty ratio differences over thousands of cycles. Measured across
Windows with numpy 1.26 and Linux with numpy 2.5, the settled output voltages
agree to about **one part per million**.

That is three orders of magnitude finer than any claim this report makes, and
roughly four orders finer than the uncertainty in the component values the
numbers are computed from, so it does not affect a single conclusion. It is
worth stating because it is the honest resolution of the simulator, and because
a reader comparing two runs digit by digit should know where to stop.

The one place it does matter is the load regulation table. The deviations there
are around 0.001 percent, which is only about ten times the solver's own
resolution. Read that column as "below what this model can resolve", not as a
measurement of 0.001 percent.

## What would change these numbers

In rough order of how much:

1. Real Rds(on), Qg, Qoss and switching times, at temperature, for real parts.
2. Real inductor core loss coefficients and DCR at temperature.
3. Layout: loop inductance in the input mesh, copper spreading for thermal,
   and the common mode path for EMC. None of it exists yet.
4. The controller's actual internal slope compensation, blanking and minimum
   on time, which this repository models generically rather than from any one
   datasheet.
